title: Safe Work Australia (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2008

divisions.question: That the amendments ( **Senator Xenophon’s** ) be agreed to.

Rachel Siewert I move Greens amendment (1) on sheet 5593: (1) Clause 26, page 16 (lines 18 to 19), omit “Division 4 allows the Ministerial Council to direct Safe Work Australia to amend either of the final plans.” This amendment relates to strategic and operational plans. As I articulated in my contribution to the second reading debate, this legislation allows the ministerial council to direct changes to strategic and operational plans of Safe Work Australia. We do not believe it is appropriate that the ministerial council should be able to directly alter strategic and operational plans. The members of the ministerial council will have representation on Safe Work Australia and will be participating in the formulation of these plans. We believe that it is unnecessary for the Commonwealth, states and territories to have direct interference in these plans. We believe that it undermines both the independence and the tripartite nature of Safe Work Australia. This amendment should be read in conjunction with Greens amendment (2), which I will move later. It also deals with strategic and operational plans and their finalisation. Basically, it takes out division 4, which allows the ministerial council to direct Safe Work Australia to amend either of the final plans. As I said, we do not believe it is appropriate to allow the ministerial council this level of interference in the operation of SWA. As I said, it undermines both the independence and tripartite approach of SWA. Eric Abetz I indicate that the opposition opposes clause 38(2) and also clause 42(2) as on sheet 5611, in the following terms. They canvass the same matters: (7) Clause 38, page 28 (lines 21 to 29), subclause (2), **TO BE OPPOSED**. (8) Clause 42, page 31 (lines 15 to 29), subclause (2), **TO BE OPPOSED**. Clause 38(1) of the legislation says: At a meeting, a question is decided by a two-thirds majority of the votes of the voting members present and voting. In relation to this legislation we think it is important that there be a general consensus in relation to matters, and therefore a matter being decided by a two-thirds majority seems to have some merit. But the legislation then goes on to say: (2) However, if the question relates to the model OHS legislation or model OHS codes of practice, the question is decided by— the two-thirds majority that I referred to before, and— (b) a majority of the votes of all of the voting members who represent the Commonwealth, States and Territories. I am assuming in my numerical calculation that the chair is in fact deemed not to be a representative of the Commonwealth and I think that would be right. In those circumstances, you would have nine votes representing the Commonwealth, states and territories—that being six for the states, two for the territories and one for the Commonwealth—and a majority of that number would of course be five out of the nine. Therefore, in the event that you had six out of the nine voting against a proposal, you could in fact have six members out of the total 14 able to defeat a matter. We believe that that will potentially give too much power to those state Labor bureaucracies that have been part and parcel of the problem, for the past decade or so, of getting good OH&S legislation in this country. speeches.speaker: Chris Evans
speeches.brief: The government moved to establish Safe Work Australia as an independent national body to improve occupational health and safety and workers' compensation, citing over 300 workplace deaths and 140,000 serious injuries annually, costing the economy $34 billion. The bill replaces the Australian Safety and Compensation Council, creates a 15-member tripartite body, and supports harmonisation of OHS laws across states and territories.

speeches.speaker: Rachel Siewert
speeches.brief: The Greens and Coalition supported the Safe Work Australia Bill 2008 but argued it reduced employer and union representation from three to two members, gave excessive control to state governments, and undermined tripartism, while Labor defended the bill as necessary to harmonise occupational health and safety laws and reduce the 4,900 annual work-related deaths and $30 billion in costs.

speeches.speaker: Mary Fisher
speeches.brief: The coalition questioned whether the bill would deliver harmonised occupational health and safety and workers' compensation laws, arguing it gave states veto power and reduced employer and union representation, while Labor supported the bill as establishing Safe Work Australia to develop national standards, citing 300 workplace deaths and 140,000 serious injuries annually.

speeches.speaker: Eric Abetz
speeches.brief: During the committee debate on the Safe Work Australia bill, the opposition and crossbench successfully moved amendments to add an objects clause, increase employer and employee representation to three members each from the ACTU and ACCI, and remove the ministerial council’s power to direct changes to strategic and operational plans. The government opposed these changes, arguing they breached the Intergovernmental Agreement and risked delaying harmonised OHS laws.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The Senate agreed to opposition amendments restricting ministerial directions to the Safe Work Australia CEO to specified non-operational matters, removed the clause allowing the minister to terminate the CEO for unsatisfactory performance, and added an audit committee for financial oversight.
